title: Out of Africa
blurb: How modern humans spread from Africa to every continent except Antarctica, meeting Neanderthals and Denisovans on the way.

steps.c: When our story begins, about 300,000 years ago, at least five kinds of human lived on Earth. Our species, Homo sapiens, will spread out of Africa and meet several of them. On the map each species has its own colour of figure, placed where its dated fossils were found. Only we are left, but most people outside Africa still carry about 2% Neanderthal DNA.

tips.t: Europe and western and central Asia, about 240,000–40,000 years ago. Relative to body size, their brains were larger than ours.
Across Asia, about 200,000–32,000 years ago, known mostly from DNA and a few bones. Tibetans' gene for coping with thin air likely came from them.
Often called Homo heidelbergensis (the name is debated). The Kabwe skull from Zambia, about 300,000 years old, lived at the same time as the first Homo sapiens.
Deep in a South African cave, 335,000–236,000 years ago: a brain a third to half the size of ours. Claims that they buried their dead are disputed.
The first humans known to leave Africa, about 2 million years ago. Their last known group lived in Java until about 117,000–108,000 years ago.
Homo floresiensis on Flores, about 1.06 m tall, lived 100,000–60,000 years ago. Homo luzonensis on Luzon is dated somewhere between about 134,000 and 50,000 years (debated).

steps.c: Fossils from Jebel Irhoud are the oldest known remains with modern-human features. Burnt flint tools found with them are dated to about 315,000 years ago (± 34,000).

tips.t: The people of Jebel Irhoud hunted mostly gazelles; hartebeest, wildebeest, zebra-like horses, rhinos, ostriches, lions and hyenas lived around them. Most are gone from Morocco today.
Rodent bones from the site point to grassland and a wetter climate than the dry farmland around the hill today.

steps.c: Near Ramla, Israel, a skull fragment and jaw about 140,000–120,000 years old belong to archaic humans, not Homo sapiens. Whether they were a distinct population or early Neanderthals is debated.

tips.t: Animals from different habitats came here to drink. Today the spot is a quarry beside a cement works.
Aurochs, horses, fallow deer and tortoises. Aurochs and wild horses have long vanished from the Levant.

steps.c: Modern humans reached the Levant long before the main dispersal: the Skhul and Qafzeh fossils in Israel are about 120,000–80,000 years old. These early groups seem to have died out or retreated.

tips.t: Shell beads worn at Qafzeh were carried from a shore about 35 km away.
Gazelles, horses, fallow and red deer, wild cattle, boar and rhinos. Wild horses, aurochs and rhinos are long gone from here.

steps.c: A bone fragment from Denisova Cave in Siberia belonged to a girl who died about 90,000 years ago, aged around 13. Her genome shows a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father.

tips.t: The Altai valley below Denisova Cave was roamed by mammoths, woolly rhinos, cave lions and cave hyenas, all now extinct. Snow leopards and dholes lived here too.

steps.c: Most ancestry of people living outside Africa today comes from one expansion about 70,000–50,000 years ago. Low sea levels narrowed the Bab-el-Mandeb strait; a northern route through Sinai and the Levant is also possible.
steps.w: Recent African origin of modern humans

tips.t: About 85,000 years ago Al Wusta, now sand desert in the Nefud, was a freshwater lake in grassland with hippos and wild cattle. A finger bone there may be Homo sapiens (debated).
Bab-el-Mandeb is 26 km wide today; when the seas fell in the Ice Age it was much narrower and shallower.

steps.c: Outside Africa, modern humans interbred with Neanderthals, probably in western Asia. Everyone with non-African ancestry carries about 1–4% Neanderthal DNA; the last major gene flow is estimated at about 65,000–47,000 years ago.
steps.w: Interbreeding between archaic and modern humans

tips.t: 640 m up in the Zagros mountains of Iraq, Neanderthals ate wild goats and butchered tortoises with flint tools.

steps.c: A child's tooth and modern-style tools at Grotte Mandrin, France, are dated to about 54,000 years ago, between Neanderthal layers. Whether this marks a short-lived visit by modern humans is debated.

tips.t: The Rhône valley below the cave linked the Mediterranean with the northern steppes. About 70,000 animal bones were found, mostly horse, bison and deer.

steps.c: Denisovans are known mainly from DNA in Denisova Cave, Siberia. Modern humans also mixed with them: about 4–6% of the genome of Melanesians comes from Denisovans, with admixture estimated at about 54,000–44,000 years ago.

tips.t: Denisovans lived in Baishiya Karst Cave on the Tibetan Plateau from about 160,000 to perhaps 32,000 years ago.
Baishiya's people hunted mostly blue sheep, plus wild yak, horses and woolly rhinos. Spotted hyenas lived there too, now gone from China.

steps.c: Australia and New Guinea, joined as Sahul by low seas, still required sea crossings. People arrived about 50,000 years ago; an earlier date of about 65,000 years at Madjedbebe is debated.

tips.t: Diprotodon, a wombat relative the size of a car, the marsupial lion, giant kangaroos, the bird Genyornis and the lizard Megalania. Most were gone by about 46,000–41,000 years ago; why is debated.
Even with seas 70–100 m lower, reaching Sahul meant several sea crossings, one of them close to 100 km.

steps.c: Modern human remains at Bacho Kiro Cave, Bulgaria, date to about 46,000–44,000 years ago, and the Zlatý kůň woman in Czechia to about 45,000 years. The Bacho Kiro people had Neanderthal ancestors only a few generations back.

tips.t: Cave bears died in Bacho Kiro Cave, and the people there wore their teeth as pendants.
About 39,500 years ago the Campanian Ignimbrite eruption spread ash over some 3 million km²; how much it cooled Europe is debated.

steps.c: Bones from Tianyuan Cave near Beijing are 42,000–39,000 years old. The genome belongs to an early branch of the East Asian lineage, related to people in East Asia and some in the Americas.

tips.t: The chemistry of Tianyuan man's bones shows that freshwater fish made up a large part of his diet.
Of 29 mammal species found in the cave, mostly deer, all still live today except the spotted hyena.

steps.c: The Yana site, north of the Arctic Circle in Siberia, shows people living there about 32,000 years ago. From this cold far north, groups later moved into Beringia, the gateway to the Americas.

tips.t: At Yana people hunted mostly reindeer, alongside mammoths, woolly rhinos, bison, horses, musk oxen and cave lions.
A nearby bone bed holds at least 26 mammoths, suggesting they mattered more than as an occasional source of ivory.

steps.c: By about 30,000 years ago, as far as the fossils show, Homo sapiens was the only human left. Neanderthals disappeared around 40,000 years ago and the Flores humans by about 50,000; the youngest Denisovan bone, from Tibet, is 48,000–32,000 years old. Why the others vanished (competition, climate, small populations, or being absorbed through interbreeding) is debated. Their genes live on in us.

tips.t: People outside Africa carry about 2% Neanderthal DNA on average; East Asians slightly more than Europeans.
Melanesians carry roughly 5% Denisovan DNA; the Ayta Magbukon of the Philippines carry the most known, about a third more than Papuans.

title: Peopling of the Americas
blurb: From the Bering land bridge to the tip of South America, and the later Arctic migrations.

steps.c: Low seas joined Siberia and Alaska into Beringia, up to 1,000 km wide. Genetics suggests the ancestors of Native Americans split from Siberians about 36,000 years ago and were isolated for thousands of years, perhaps in Beringia.

tips.t: Beringia stayed free of ice because so little snow fell. Moist Pacific air kept a refuge of shrub tundra, with patches of larch, amid grassy steppe.
Cut marks on animal bones in these Yukon caves may show people here about 24,000 years ago. The dates are disputed because the layers are uncertain.

steps.c: At the Last Glacial Maximum, about 26,000–20,000 years ago, ice sheets covered most of Canada. By 21,000 years ago the Cordilleran and Laurentide sheets had joined, blocking an inland route south.

tips.t: The Laurentide ice sheet was up to 3 km thick over northern Quebec, thinning towards its edges. It gouged out the basins of the five Great Lakes.
Later, 15,000–13,000 years ago, an ice-dammed lake in Montana burst again and again. The largest flood carried about 13 times the flow of the Amazon.

steps.c: Human footprints on the shore of ancient Lake Otero, New Mexico, were dated to about 23,000–21,000 years ago. If correct, people were south of the ice during the glacial maximum; the dates are debated.

tips.t: The same mudflats hold tracks of Columbian mammoths, ground sloths, American lions and dire wolves. One sloth reared on its hind legs and spun around.
Most prints were made by teenagers and children. In one trail an older person set a child down and picked it up again, slipping under the extra weight.

steps.c: As the ice retreated, the Pacific coast of Alaska and British Columbia opened up, roughly 16,000–15,000 years ago. Rich kelp forests may have fed people travelling south by boat.

tips.t: On a small island off British Columbia, a hearth was radiocarbon dated to between 13,613 and 14,086 years old.
A man who died in his mid-twenties in On Your Knees Cave, Alaska, about 9,800 years ago, ate almost only marine food. His obsidian came from British Columbia.

steps.c: A campsite with wooden structures in southern Chile, usually dated to about 14,500 years ago, showed people had reached South America before Clovis. A 2026 study argues for a much younger age; this is debated.

tips.t: Hearths held nine species of seaweed and marine algae, and the camp had a 13,000-year-old wild potato and remains of 45 edible plant species.
People butchered Notiomastodon, an extinct elephant relative called a gomphothere. A peat bog later sealed the camp, preserving wood, hides and plants.

steps.c: Human coprolites (preserved dung) with human DNA from Paisley Caves are dated to about 14,300 years ago, evidence for people before Clovis. Some of these dates are contested.

tips.t: Bones of extinct camels, horses and bison lay with the dung layers, alongside many bones of waterfowl and fish.
People here made Western Stemmed points, quite unlike Clovis points. The caves sit above the Summer Lake basin, shaped by Ice Age lake waves.

steps.c: A passage opened between the shrinking ice sheets east of the Rockies about 13,800 years ago. It may only have been usable for people somewhat later, so it probably was not the first route south.

tips.t: Charlie Lake Cave, British Columbia, held a fluted point and two buried ravens, called the oldest traces of ritual in Canada; finds go back 10,500–11,000 years.
A 2016 study found the corridor became liveable only slowly; Clovis people probably came from the south, perhaps following bison, not down the corridor.

steps.c: Clovis points, first found at Blackwater Draw, New Mexico, spread widely about 13,050–12,750 years ago. The Anzick child in Montana, buried with Clovis tools, is closely related to living Native Americans.

tips.t: Ridgley Whiteman of Clovis recognised the site in 1929. Gravel mining in 1952–1970 exposed mammoth and bison kill sites; camel, horse and sabre-toothed cat remains occur too.
The Anzick child, 1–2 years old, lay with over 115 stone and antler tools dusted with red ochre. It was reburied in an intertribal ceremony in 2014.

steps.c: Paleo-Eskimo peoples spread across the Arctic from about 3900 BCE. The Thule, ancestors of the Inuit, expanded east from Alaska after about 1000 CE and reached Greenland by the 13th century, replacing the Dorset.

tips.t: Thule people collected iron from meteorites, such as the Cape York meteorite in Greenland, worked it and traded it between communities.
Inuit legends tell of the Tuniit, taller and stronger than Inuit but shy: a memory of the Dorset. Dorset people had no bows or arrows.

title: Doggerland drowns
blurb: How rising seas turned the land between Britain and the continent into the North Sea.

steps.c: With sea level about 120 m lower, dry land linked Britain to the continent. Ice covered the northern half of the British Isles and crossed Doggerland towards Denmark.

tips.t: Trawlers on the Dogger Bank have dredged up moor peat and remains of mammoth and rhinoceros, animals of the open plains that once stood here.
The Dogger Bank hill is a thrust moraine: ground shoved up by the ice sheet during the Last Glacial Maximum.

steps.c: During the cold Younger Dryas, about 12,900–11,700 years ago, Ahrensburg hunters followed reindeer across the North European plain, now partly under the sea. At Stellmoor, bones of about 650 reindeer were found.

tips.t: At Stellmoor, intact reindeer skeletons were found with flint arrowheads in the chest, perhaps sacrifices. Arrow shafts of pine wood survived too.
Stellmoor was a seasonal camp, used mainly in October, when the reindeer herds passed.

steps.c: Hunter-gatherers lived by a lake at Star Carr from about 9300 to 8500 BCE. Finds include antler headdresses, a timber platform and one of Britain's oldest known houses.

tips.t: A small engraved shale pendant found here in 2015 is thought to be the oldest known Mesolithic art in Britain.
People hunted red and roe deer, elk, aurochs and wild boar. The site's 195 barbed points are over 95% of all known from Mesolithic Britain.

steps.c: Doggerland was a lowland of rivers, marshes and lagoons, used by Mesolithic hunters and fishers. Between 10,000 and 7,000 years ago rising seas broke it into islands.

tips.t: Streams from the Dogger hills drained into a lake in the Outer Silver Pit, today a basin between two huge sandbanks.

steps.c: By about 6500 BCE the sea had cut Britain off from the mainland.

tips.t: A man buried in Gough's Cave, Somerset, about 8300 BCE, probably had dark skin and blue-green eyes, and could not digest milk as an adult.
At Bouldnor Cliff, 11 m under the Solent, a lobster was seen throwing worked flints out of its burrow. The drowned site is about 8,000 years old.

steps.c: About 6200 BCE an undersea landslide off Norway sent a tsunami across the North Sea, leaving sediment up to 29 km inland in Scotland. Its effect on the remaining Doggerland is debated.

tips.t: About 290 km of the Norwegian shelf edge collapsed, sending some 3,500 km³ of debris downslope. Studies for the Ormen Lange gas field mapped it closely.
In the Montrose Basin and Firth of Forth a grey tsunami sand layer lies between peat, reaching 4 m above today's normal tide level.

steps.c: The higher ground of Dogger Bank survived as an island until at least about 5000 BCE, before it too disappeared below the waves.

tips.t: The bank takes its name from doggers, two-masted medieval Dutch fishing boats that trawled here for cod and herring.
The bank covers about 17,600 km², some 160 by 60 miles, under only about 15–36 m of water. It is now planned as a giant offshore wind area.

steps.c: In 1931 the trawler Colinda hauled up a lump of peat near the Leman and Ower banks, off Norfolk. Inside was a barbed antler point, proof that people once lived on what is now sea floor.

tips.t: Also in 1931, a magnitude 6.1 earthquake struck at the Dogger Bank, the largest ever recorded in the United Kingdom.
A Neanderthal skull fragment over 40,000 years old was recovered from the seabed about 10 miles off the coast of Zeeland, Netherlands.

title: Polynesian wayfinding
blurb: How Austronesian seafarers from Taiwan settled the remote Pacific, from Lapita pottery makers to the last great voyages to Rapa Nui and Aotearoa.

steps.c: Austronesian-speaking farmers and seafarers spread south from Taiwan from about 3000 BCE. They reached the Batanes Islands of the northern Philippines by about 2200 BCE and went on to settle island Southeast Asia.

tips.t: Before 1500 CE, Austronesian languages reached from Madagascar to Easter Island. About 386 million people speak them today.
Austronesians sailed catamarans and outrigger boats with the crab claw sail; sails were in use before 2000 BCE.

steps.c: About 1500 BCE the Lapita culture, known for finely stamped pottery, appears in the Bismarck Archipelago. Its seafarers then crossed into islands no humans had reached, such as Vanuatu, where the Teouma cemetery was in use about 1000 BCE.

tips.t: Some Lapita houses stood on stilts over large lagoons. Talepakemalai on Mussau is one of the earliest Lapita sites in the Bismarcks.
At Teouma, skulls were removed after death and replaced with cone shell rings. DNA of the buried women is closest to the Ami and Atayal of Taiwan.

steps.c: By about 900–800 BCE Lapita seafarers had settled Fiji, Tonga and Samoa, the first islands of what is now called Polynesia.

tips.t: Nukuleka on Tongatapu may be Tonga's first settlement. A coral file found there was dated to 888 BC by uranium–thorium.
Lapita settlers kept pigs, dogs and chickens, and traded obsidian over long distances.

steps.c: Then the eastward movement stopped. For about 1,500 years or more, West Polynesia remained the edge of the settled Pacific, and Lapita pottery-making faded. Why voyaging paused so long is debated.

tips.t: The Polynesian rat cannot swim far, so its bones and DNA trace human voyages across the Pacific. Its DNA suggests it came from Flores.

steps.c: Around 1000 CE voyagers reached the Society Islands and their neighbours. Radiocarbon studies (Wilmshurst et al. 2011) suggest East Polynesia was settled later and faster than once thought; older estimates are centuries earlier.

tips.t: This marae may date from about 1000 CE. Navigators gathered here, and a stone taken from it founded new marae elsewhere. UNESCO World Heritage since 2017.

steps.c: Far to the north, Polynesians settled Hawaiʻi. A recent survey of radiocarbon dates puts first arrival at about 940–1130 CE; other estimates range from the 1200s to centuries earlier.

tips.t: Regular canoe voyages linked Tahiti and Hawaiʻi for some time but stopped around 1300 CE. By 1778 about 300,000 people lived on the islands (estimate).
Polynesian rats came too. On Oʻahu they caused a decline of native palms and shrubs in the lowland forests.

steps.t: Rapa Nui, far to the east
steps.c: Rapa Nui (Easter Island) was colonised late, about 1200 CE according to current best estimates. Earlier researchers often cited about 800 CE.

tips.t: More than 900 moai are known, on average 4 m tall and 12.5 tonnes, carved mostly 1250–1500. Nearly half remain at the Rano Raraku quarry.
Fossils show a giant palm, Paschalococos, once dominated the island; by 1722 no tree stood above about 3 m. Pitcairn, the nearest inhabited land, is 2,075 km away.

steps.c: East Polynesians carry a trace of Native American ancestry, closest to the Zenú of Colombia, from contact about 1150–1230 CE (Ioannidis et al. 2020). The South American sweet potato also reached Polynesia before Europeans. Where contact happened is debated.

tips.t: Quechua names for sweet potato, such as kumar, are strikingly like the Polynesian kumara; some scholars see this as a sign of contact (debated).
The earliest sweet potato remains in Mangaia, Cook Islands, are dated to 1210–1400 CE, before any European ship reached the Pacific.

steps.c: New Zealand was settled from East Polynesia about 1250–1300 CE. No human traces can be safely dated before the Kaharoa ash of about 1314 CE, and mitochondrial DNA points to 1250–1300.

tips.t: The largest moa stood about 3.6 m tall and weighed about 230 kg; their only predator was Haast's eagle. All moa were extinct by 1445.
Bones of the Polynesian rat, kiore, were once dated to over 2,000 years ago; later work showed it reached both main islands about 1280.

steps.c: In 1976 the voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa sailed from Maui to Tahiti in about 34 days, navigated without instruments by Mau Piailug of Satawal. The voyage helped revive traditional Polynesian wayfinding.

tips.t: Launched in 1975, Hōkūleʻa is 18.7 m long and carries 12–16 crew. It was built to test whether Polynesians settled the Pacific by purposeful voyaging.
In 2014–2017 Hōkūleʻa sailed 47,000 nautical miles round the world, calling at 85 ports in 26 countries.

title: Five ice ages
blurb: How the planet breathed over 500,000 years: ice sheets came and went, seas rose and fell, the Sahara turned green and dried again.

steps.c: For the last half-million years Earth has swung between long ice ages and short warm spells, roughly every 100,000 years. Since about 430,000 years ago (the Mid-Brunhes Event) the swings have been especially deep. Why the weak 100,000-year wobble of Earth's orbit sets the beat is still an open question: the "100,000-year problem".
steps.img: Woolly mammoth

tips.t: Bubbles in Antarctic ice drilled at Dome C hold ancient air: in 800,000 years, CO2 never topped the levels seen since industrialisation. Today it is about 50 percent higher.
In 1967 Nicholas Shackleton argued that oxygen isotopes in fossil seafloor shells mainly track the volume of ice on land. That idea underlies the numbered marine isotope stages.

steps.c: In the Anglian glaciation (MIS 12), the harshest in Britain for two million years, ice reached Finchley and Hornchurch in north London and pushed the Thames south into its present valley. A lake dammed behind the ice spilled over the chalk ridge joining Britain to France in giant waterfalls: the first breach of the Dover Strait.
steps.img: Anglian stage

tips.t: Just before this ice age, about 480,000 years ago, people at Boxgrove butchered a 600 kg horse on a tidal mudflat below chalk cliffs, knapping flint tools on the spot.

tips.h: Ice to the Isles of Scilly
tips.t: Anglian ice reached the Isles of Scilly and the Western Approaches: the furthest south ice reached in Britain in any Pleistocene ice age.

steps.c: MIS 11 was the longest warm spell of the last 500,000 years. Southern Greenland lost most of its ice and seas may have stood 6 to 20 m higher (estimates vary). DNA of pine, yew and butterflies under 2 km of Greenland ice is at least 450,000 years old; whether it comes from this warm spell is debated. In Suffolk, people were making fire about 400,000 years ago.
steps.img: Marine Isotope Stage 11

tips.t: The Clacton Spear, a yew point found at Clacton-on-Sea in 1911, is about 400,000 years old: the oldest known worked wooden weapon. Oak forest and grassland lined its river.
At Swanscombe, where pieces of an early Neanderthal skull turned up in 1935-1955, the same river gravels hold Barbary macaques, straight-tusked elephants, rhinos and beavers.

steps.t: The Saalian ice reaches the Rhine
steps.c: In the penultimate ice age (MIS 6) Scandinavian ice crossed the Netherlands and reached the Rhine near Düsseldorf; the Hondsrug ridge in Drenthe was shaped under it. A second megaflood through the Dover Strait, dated to about 160,000 years ago by inference, finished cutting the chalk ridge: since then Britain becomes an island whenever the sea is high.
steps.img: Saale glaciation

tips.t: Drenthe's 52 hunebeds, Neolithic tombs, are built from boulders this ice carried from Sweden and Finland. The largest stones weigh around 40 tonnes.

steps.c: The last interglacial (Eemian) was as warm as today or up to 2 °C warmer, and seas stood 6 to 9 m higher; Scandinavia was an island. Hippos wallowed as far north as Teesside in northern England, and straight-tusked elephants roamed Europe. Builders in the 1950s found hippo, lion and elephant bones right under Trafalgar Square. The Sahara was green.
steps.img: Last Interglacial

tips.t: Kirkdale Cave held Eemian bones of hippos, elephants, rhinos and cave lions dragged in by hyenas, plus fossil dung. In 1821 Buckland showed it was a den, not Noah's Flood.
At Neumark-Nord in Germany lie at least 57 straight-tusked elephants butchered by Neanderthals; researchers estimate one was killed every 5 to 6 years over about 300 years.

steps.c: Toba on Sumatra, the largest known explosive eruption of the last 2.6 million years, threw out about 3,800 km³ of rock, leaving ash 5 cm deep across India and glass shards as far as South Africa; the crater is now Lake Toba. It was once thought to have nearly wiped out humankind, but most recent evidence argues against that: stone tools in India and South Africa carry on above the ash.
steps.img: Youngest Toba eruption

tips.t: Samosir, 630 km² in the middle of Lake Toba, is the largest island within an island. Lake sediments show it has risen at least 450 m since the eruption.
Toba ash at least 1 cm thick covered more than 38 million km², about 7.5% of Earth's surface; on the central Indian Ocean floor it lies 10 cm thick.

steps.c: The last ice age was not steady. Greenland ice cores record 25 Dansgaard–Oeschger events: warmings of 5 °C, and up to about 16 °C, within a few decades, followed by slow cooling. In Heinrich events armadas of icebergs broke off the North American ice through Hudson Strait and dropped Canadian rock on the sea floor off Europe. The cause is still debated.
steps.img: Dansgaard–Oeschger event

tips.t: In 1992 the GRIP team reached bedrock at Summit, the top of the Greenland ice sheet, with a 3,029 m core. Its isotopes made the abrupt glacial climate jumps clear.
Under Dye 3, a Cold War radar station on the ice, Danish drillers hit bedrock at 2,038 m in 1981; ice from the last glaciation began at 1,785 m.

steps.c: About 21,000 years ago the world was on average about 6 °C colder (estimates range from 4 to 6 °C) and sea level about 125 m lower. Ice over Canada was over 3 km thick. Doggerland, Beringia, Sundaland and Sahul were dry land, and the mammoth steppe ran from Spain to the Yukon, the largest biome on Earth. Ice cores from then hold 20 to 25 times more dust than today: a windy, dry world.
steps.img: Mammoth steppe

tips.h: Painted cave, now under the sea
tips.t: Cosquer Cave near Marseille was painted when the sea was far lower; its entrance now lies 37 m underwater. Among its animals are 9 seals and 3 great auks.
South of the ice sheets, permafrost covered Europe as far south as present-day Szeged in southern Hungary.

steps.c: An ice dam in Montana held back Lake Missoula, then burst again and again: dozens of floods, each pouring up to 10 km³ of water an hour across Washington State, carved the Channeled Scablands and the 5.6 km-wide Dry Falls. Their dates differ between studies, roughly 18,000 to 13,000 years ago. J Harlen Bretz, who proposed the floods in 1923, was ridiculed for decades before he was proved right.
steps.img: Missoula floods

tips.t: At Camas Prairie, Montana, the floods left current ripples 25 to 50 ft (8-15 m) high and 300 ft long: key evidence for Bretz's floods.
The 14-tonne Willamette Meteorite, the largest found in the US, lay in Oregon with no crater. It probably rode an ice raft from Canada or Montana in the floods.

steps.c: When the climate warmed suddenly about 14,600 years ago, sea level rose 16 to 25 m in about 400 to 500 years, 40 to 60 mm a year (today about 3 mm). Wide coastal plains such as the Sunda Shelf went under. Which ice sheets the water came from is still unresolved.

tips.t: A great river, the North Sunda or Molengraaff River, drained the dry shelf. Its fish, the river threadfin, still lives in rivers of Borneo and Sumatra.
Some researchers think a 50-150 km wide savanna corridor ran from the Malay Peninsula through Sumatra and Java to Borneo; others think rainforest dominated.

steps.t: The Younger Dryas: back into the cold
steps.c: About 12,900 years ago the North Atlantic world plunged back into near-glacial cold: Greenland cooled by up to 10 °C within a few decades, Europe by 2 to 6 °C. The usual explanation is a weakening of the Atlantic overturning circulation, perhaps after meltwater from Lake Agassiz. It ended about 11,700 years ago, with Greenland warming about 8 °C in 40 years. It is named after a small alpine flower.
steps.img: Younger Dryas

tips.t: At Stellmoor near Hamburg, autumn hunters left bones of 650 reindeer, pine arrow shafts, and whole reindeer skeletons with flint arrowheads in their chests.
In Britain, where it is called the Loch Lomond Stadial, icefields and glaciers grew again in the uplands, and lowland permafrost implies mean yearly temperatures no higher than -1 °C.

steps.c: In the African Humid Period stronger monsoon rains turned much of the Sahara into grassland with lakes, hippos, crocodiles and giraffes. Lake Mega-Chad covered at least 360,000 km², by some estimates more than the Caspian Sea. In the Cave of Swimmers in Egypt's desert, painted figures appear to swim.
steps.img: Cave of Swimmers

tips.h: A family grave by a lake
tips.t: At Gobero in Niger's desert, fishers lived by a lake 3 km wide. A woman and two children lie facing each other, hands entwined; pollen hints at flowers.
Wadi Howar, a dry valley over 1,100 km long, was then a Nile tributary. The Sahara's southern edge lay some 500 km further north than today.

steps.c: About 8,200 years ago the last great ice-dammed lakes, Agassiz and Ojibway, probably drained into the North Atlantic. Greenland cooled by about 3 °C in under 20 years; the cold spell lasted about 150 years, and sea level jumped by between 0.5 and 4 m.

tips.h: A lake bigger than the Caspian
tips.t: At its largest, Lake Agassiz may have covered 440,000 km², more than any lake today. Lake Winnipeg and Lake of the Woods are its leftovers.
About 6225-6170 BCE, 3,500 km³ of seabed slid off Norway's shelf, sending a tsunami across the North Atlantic to Britain and Doggerland.

steps.c: Between about 6,000 and 5,000 years ago the monsoon retreated and the green Sahara turned to desert. Whether this happened abruptly or gradually and region by region is debated. Herders and their cattle, painted on the rocks of Tassili n'Ajjer, moved toward the Nile and the Sahel.
steps.img: African humid period

tips.t: From 5500 BC herders at Nabta Playa buried cattle in clay-lined, roofed chambers under stone mounds, and raised a stone circle that may be an early sky calendar.
In Chad, with under 2 mm of rain a year, 18 Ounianga lakes live on groundwater stored in the wet millennia. Lake Yoa evaporates 6 m a year.

steps.c: A megadrought in the 22nd century BCE is one of the most severe climate events of our epoch. It may have helped bring down the Akkadian Empire and Egypt's Old Kingdom, though how much is debated, and it was not global. It marks the start of the Meghalayan, the age we live in, named after a stalagmite in a cave in India.
steps.img: Meghalayan

tips.t: At Tell Leilan in Syria, an Akkadian-era city, about 1 m of sediment with no trace of people covers the ruins; excavators link it to a three-century drought.
Fossil corals from Oman suggest longer winter shamal wind seasons around 2200 BC, which could have salted irrigated fields; their role in Akkad's fall is debated.

title: The spread of farming
blurb: How farming began independently in several parts of the world after the Ice Age and spread from the Fertile Crescent across Europe.

steps.c: From about 12,500 BCE, Natufian people of the Levant lived in settled villages, harvesting wild cereals and hunting gazelle. The cold, dry Younger Dryas (about 10,900–9,700 BCE) may have pushed them toward cultivation; this idea is debated.

tips.t: At Ain Mallaha by ancient Lake Hula, a woman was buried with her hand resting on a puppy: the earliest known archaeological evidence of dog domestication.
At Raqefet Cave on Mount Carmel, stone mortars may have been used to brew cereal beer about 13,000 years ago, and graves were lined with flowers like Judean sage (interpretations).

steps.c: Around 9500 BCE people at Göbekli Tepe raised huge carved stone pillars. They were hunter-gatherers who may already have used early domestic cereals. Whether settled life led to farming or the reverse is still debated.

tips.t: The pillars, the oldest known megaliths, are carved with lions, bulls, boars, foxes, gazelles, snakes, insects, spiders and above all vultures. Some have human arms.
About 60 km away lies a sister site: more than 266 T-shaped pillars were counted at Karahan Tepe, along with carved human heads and a 2.3 m statue.

steps.c: In the Fertile Crescent, people domesticated the 'founder crops': einkorn and emmer wheat, barley, lentils, peas and flax. Sheep, goats, cattle and pigs were domesticated here about 10,000–11,000 years ago.

tips.t: DNA fingerprinting suggests einkorn wheat was first domesticated near Karacadağ in south-east Turkey, an area with a number of early farming villages.
Çayönü may be where pigs were first domesticated. Its people also ran a copper and malachite workshop around 6900-6800 BCE, making copper beads.

steps.c: Çatalhöyük in central Anatolia, founded about 7100 BCE, flourished around 7000 BCE as one of the largest early farming settlements. Recent work suggests 600–800 residents at a time, far fewer than once estimated.

tips.t: There were no streets: houses packed like a honeycomb were entered through roof holes by ladders. The dead were buried beneath floors, platforms and hearths.
A mural is often called the oldest map: houses beneath the twin peaks of Mount Hasan, perhaps erupting. Critics see a leopard skin and geometric patterns instead.

steps.c: Farming was invented independently in the New Guinea highlands. At Kuk Swamp, drainage ditches go back about 9,000 years, and bananas were deliberately planted by about 6,900–6,400 years ago. Earlier dates for taro are debated.

tips.t: Kuk lies at about 1,550 m in the Wahgi Valley. Wooden digging sticks and a grindstone lay in its ditches; the Kawelka people live there today.
The best evidence points to New Guinea as where Papuans first domesticated sugarcane. Kuk shows sugar cane, with bananas, being grown 6,900-6,400 years ago.

steps.c: In Mexico, maize was domesticated from wild teosinte about 9,000 years ago, most likely in the Balsas River valley. In the Andes, farmers around Lake Titicaca domesticated the potato about 10,000–7,000 years ago.

tips.t: In Guilá Naquitz cave, Oaxaca, domesticated squash dates to 8,000-10,750 years ago, about 4,000 years before maize and beans there.
Andean farmers made chuño: small potatoes left out about three nights to freeze, drying by day. Remains have been found at Tiwanaku near Lake Titicaca.

steps.c: Rice was first domesticated in the Yangtze valley, probably about 9,000 years ago (estimates vary widely). In the north, the Cishan culture (6500–5000 BCE) grew broomcorn millet and stored it in hundreds of pits.

tips.t: At Jiahu (about 7000-5700 BC), people buried 33 flutes carved from red-crowned crane wing bones, among the oldest playable instruments in the world.
Later, at Hemudu near Hangzhou Bay (from 5500 BC), rice farmers lived in long stilt houses, tilled with shoulder-blade hoes and made red lacquer bowls.

steps.c: Farming reached Greece about 7000–6500 BCE, brought by farmers expanding from the Aegean and the Near East. The Karanovo culture in Bulgaria and the Starčevo–Körös–Criș culture spread village farming across the Balkans.

tips.t: At Lepenski Vir in the Danube's Iron Gates gorge, fishers carved fish-faced stone heads and built trapezoid houses (6300-6000 BC) as newly arrived farmers mixed with them.
Nea Nikomedeia (6250-6050 BC), one of Europe's oldest farming villages, had 12 m square timber houses and jars holding up to 85 litres, on a shore now inland.

steps.c: Cardial (impressed-ware) farmers spread by sea along the Mediterranean, from western Greece about 6400 BCE to Portugal. From about 5500 BCE, Linear Pottery (LBK) farmers settled central Europe from Hungary to the Paris Basin.

tips.t: Linear Pottery longhouses, built on fertile loess near rivers, were the largest free-standing buildings in the world at the time. Their builders favoured cattle.
Near Kückhoven in Germany, a timber-lined Linear Pottery well built around 5100 BC is one of the oldest wooden structures in the world.

steps.c: Farming reached Britain and Ireland about 4000 BCE with incoming farmers who largely replaced local hunter-gatherers. In southern Scandinavia the Funnelbeaker culture took up farming from about 4100 BCE.

tips.t: The Sweet Track crossed Somerset's peat bog on timbers felled in 3807 BC, dated by tree rings. A ceremonial jadeitite axe head was found along it.
Cheddar Man, a hunter-gatherer of about 8300 BC, probably had dark skin and blue-green eyes (limited DNA). Farmers later brought lighter skin and brown eyes.

steps.c: Africa's Sahel had its own crops. Domesticated pearl millet appears in northern Mali by about 2500–2000 BCE, and the Sahel is its suggested area of domestication.

tips.t: From about 2000 BCE herders and farmers on the Dhar Tichitt cliffs in Mauritania built drystone compounds with granaries; pearl millet was their only domesticated crop.
At Ounjougou in Mali, pottery appears in the first half of the 10th millennium BC: the earliest found in Africa, made to cook grains.

title: From wild plants and animals to dinner
blurb: How foragers' wild grasses, pods and tubers became wheat, rice, maize and potatoes, how wild sheep, aurochs and boars became farm animals, and how both travelled the world.

steps.c: About 23,000 years ago fisher-hunter-gatherers camped on the shore of the Sea of Galilee. They left over 90,000 seeds from more than 100 plant species. Wild barley and grasses were ground into flour on a stone slab, and flint blades show sickle wear. No fields yet: every grain came from wild plants that shed their seed.
steps.img: Crop: Barley

tips.t: The Ohalo II foragers also gathered wild lentils, whose pods burst open to scatter their seeds, some 12,000 years before lentils were cultivated.
Starch on stone tools shows taro was used at Kilu Cave, Solomon Islands, some 28,000–20,000 years ago.

steps.c: At Shubayqa 1 in Jordan's Black Desert, Natufian foragers baked something like flatbread 14,400 years ago. Charred crumbs hold flour of wild einkorn, barley or oats mixed with ground club-rush tubers. Wild wheat had tough husks and ears that fell apart, so this was hard-won food, baked 4,000 years before farming began.
steps.img: Crop: Einkorn wheat

tips.t: Natufian foragers (c. 12,500–9500 BCE) gathered wild cereals, legumes, almonds, acorns and pistachios, and hunted mountain gazelle.
In Japan, Jōmon foragers made the world's oldest pottery, c. 14,500 BCE, and ate chestnuts, acorns with the tannins processed out, salmon and shellfish.

steps.c: At Abu Hureyra in Syria, foragers harvested 'wild gardens' of einkorn, emmer and rye and hunted gazelle. Some archaeologists think they were already sowing rye around 11,050 BCE, in the cold Younger Dryas (debated). Domestic-type einkorn appears only after about 8800 BCE: people tended wild cereals for over a thousand years before the plants changed.
steps.img: Crop: Einkorn wheat

tips.t: Models once claimed domestication could take only 20–200 years. Archaeology shows over a thousand years of cultivating wild plants first.
Wild einkorn is a short grass under 70 cm. Its ripe ears shatter, dropping kernels wrapped in tough husks; the crop's ears stay whole for reaping.

steps.c: Around 9500 BCE people at Göbekli Tepe raised carved stone pillars and processed cereals on a huge scale: over 7,000 grinding stones survive. Gazelle were hunted from midsummer to autumn amid stands of wild einkorn and barley. Whether the grain was still gathered wild or already sown is unclear.
steps.img: Crop: Barley

tips.t: DNA fingerprinting traces domesticated einkorn to Karaca Dağ, a range of hills less than 100 km east of Göbekli Tepe.
Nine seedless figs from Gilgal I near Jericho, c. 9400–9200 BC, may come from planted trees: perhaps the oldest crop of all (debated).

steps.c: By about 7500 BCE villages across the Fertile Crescent grew seven founder crops: einkorn, emmer, barley, lentil, pea, chickpea and flax. Wild ears shattered and wild pods burst open; the crops held their seed until harvest, so it could be reaped. Grain gave bread and porridge, pulses added protein, and flax gave oil and linen.
steps.img: Crop: Emmer wheat

tips.t: At Yiftah'el, Israel, archaeologists found a hoard of more than one million carbonised lentils about 10,000 years old.
The chickpea's wild relative grows only in a small area of SE Turkey and nearby Syria; its small seeds ripen unevenly and need a rest before sprouting.
In the Zagros and upper Euphrates hunters began sparing female goats, sheep and aurochs and culling young males. Bones still looked wild for centuries, but the herd profile shows herding.
Early farmers shipped sheep, goats, pigs, cattle and even a cat to Cyprus, an island with none of them. Domestic animals travelled with people from the start.

steps.t: Rice in the south, millet north
steps.c: Wild rice in the Yangtze marshes dropped its grains as they ripened, and wild foxtail grass did the same. Farmers slowly favoured plants that held their seed. Rice grew near Shangshan and Hemudu, while broomcorn and foxtail millet filled storage pits at Cishan (early dates debated). Drought-hardy millet became East Asia's first dry-land crop.
steps.img: Crop: Asian rice

tips.t: Between 6,900 and 6,600 years ago, rice ears that keep their grain rose only from 27% to 39% of the harvest.
Wild soybeans at Jiahu had small seeds. Large-seeded soybeans appear in Japan by 5,000 and in Korea by 3,000 years ago.

steps.c: Independently of anyone else, people at Kuk Swamp dug ditches about 9,000 years ago to drain the wetland for taro. Raw wild taro is acrid with needle-like crystals, and wild bananas are packed with hard seeds and little pulp. By around 5000 BCE farmers were deliberately planting bananas; seedless bananas grown from suckers came later.
steps.img: Crop: Banana

tips.t: Papuans and Austronesians first grew sugarcane, bred from wild New Guinea cane, mainly as food for their domesticated pigs.
Taro starch turns up at Lapita sites of 1100–550 BC; in Hawaii, Polynesian settlers later made it into poi.

steps.c: In Mexico's Balsas valley, teosinte was a bushy grass whose tiny ears held 5–10 seeds in stone-hard cases. Over thousands of years farmers turned it into maize: one tall stalk, and cobs of naked kernels that stay put. Squash came even earlier at Guilá Naquitz, bred from small bitter gourds into fleshy fruit.
steps.img: Crop: Maize

tips.t: Maize and teosinte look so different that teosinte was only proposed as maize's ancestor in 1931–32; two genes explain much of the change.
Wild squashes were probably spread by mammoths and mastodons; after these giants died out, people became their seed dispersers.

steps.c: South America tamed its own crops. Near Lake Titicaca farmers bred small wild tubers laced with toxic glycoalkaloids into big, safe potatoes; tubers from 2500 BCE survive at Ancón. Andean beans grew larger, cassava swelled into starchy roots on the Amazon's southern fringe, and cacao was grown in Ecuador's upper Amazon 5,300 years ago.
steps.img: Crop: Potato

tips.t: Bitter cassava needs careful processing to remove cyanide, yet farmers may choose bitter varieties because they lose less of the crop.
Cacao was probably first grown for the sweet white pulp around its bitter seeds, eaten as a snack or made into a mild alcoholic drink.
In the high Andes, llamas, alpacas and guinea pigs were domesticated independently of the Old World; llama dung fuelled and fertilised life above 4,000 m.

steps.c: Fruit trees took patience. Wild olives had small, thin-fleshed fruit; wild vines had separate male and female plants. Growers cloned the best olives from cuttings and grafts, and hand-pollinated date palms. Oil, wine and dates followed: Crete stored olive oil in amphorae by 3500 BCE. Tea (China) and coffee (Yemen) came much later.
steps.img: Crop: Olive

tips.t: Armenia's Areni-1 cave held a winery about 6,000 years old, with a wine press, fermentation vats, jars and cups.
The oldest tea leaves come from the tomb of Han Emperor Jing (died 141 BC) near Xi'an; Yemen grew coffee by the 15th century AD.
Thousands of years after domestication, people learned to use living animals: milk, wool, ploughing and carts. Wool sheep and milking spread across Eurasia in the 4th millennium BCE.

steps.c: African farmers tamed grasses of the savanna and Sahel whose wild heads shattered. Sorghum was domesticated near Kassala by 3500–3000 BCE, pearl millet in Mali's Tilemsi Valley by 2500 BCE, and African rice in the Inner Niger Delta about 3,000 years ago. Further south, people grew white yams and used oil palm fruit.
steps.img: Crop: Sorghum

tips.t: A piece of sorghum bread from a Predynastic Egyptian grave, about 5,100 years old, is kept in Turin's Egyptian Museum.
White yams grow from pieces of tuber, so farmers keep up to 30% of each harvest to replant; many wild yams are toxic.

steps.c: Crops now travelled far from home. Wheat reached China's lower Yellow River around 2600 BCE and barley Korea by 1500 BCE. Broomcorn millet went west, reaching central Europe in the second millennium BCE. Sorghum reached India about 4,000 years ago, sugarcane by 1000 BCE, and cotton was spun in Nubia and grown in Han Yunnan.

tips.t: Though domesticated in China by 6000 BC, foxtail millet only shows up for certain in the Near East in the Iron Age, at Tille Höyük.
The Greek envoy Megasthenes told Seleucus I of Indian 'trees on which wool grows', probably tree cotton.

steps.c: After 1492 ships carried crops both ways across the Atlantic. Chilies reached Spain in 1493 and Goa by 1520; maize grew in Spain around 1525, tomatoes in Italy by 1544, potatoes in Spain around 1570. Westward went wheat, sown in Mexico in the 1520s, and sugarcane, first harvested on Hispaniola in 1501.
steps.img: Crop: Tomato

tips.t: In 1548 Cosimo de' Medici's steward reported a basket of tomatoes had arrived safely, yet Tuscans long used them only to decorate tables.
African rice reached Brazil on slave ships by about the 1550s; enslaved West Africans brought both the seed and the skill to grow it.

steps.c: Potatoes fed Europe's growing villages: Ireland rose from about 2 million people in 1700 to 8 million. Then blight struck in 1845; in 1846 three-quarters of the harvest was lost. About a million died and over a million emigrated. Today a few crops feed most of us: rice alone is the staple of over half the world.
steps.img: Crop: Potato

tips.t: France's yearly potato crop soared from 21 million hectolitres in 1815 to 117 million in 1840, letting its population grow.
Sugarcane is the heaviest crop (1.9 billion t, 2020), maize the top grain (1.16 billion t), and wheat covers more land than any other food crop.

title: Bronze Age collapse
blurb: How a connected world of kings, traders and palaces around the eastern Mediterranean came apart around 1200 BCE, and what grew from the ruins.

steps.c: In the mid-14th century BCE the pharaohs at Amarna exchanged letters and gifts with the kings of Babylon, Assyria, Mitanni, the Hittites and Cyprus, calling one another 'brother'. The archive covers only about 15–30 years.

tips.t: Around 1887 a local woman digging old mud-brick for fertiliser at Amarna found over 300 clay tablets. Most are letters in Akkadian, the diplomatic language of the age.
Tushratta, king of Mitanni, complained that Egypt sent him gold-plated statues instead of solid gold ones, part of the bride-price for his daughter Tadukhepa.

steps.c: About 1320 BCE a merchant ship sank off Uluburun in southern Turkey. It carried about 10 tons of Cypriot copper and 1 ton of tin, enough for 11 tons of bronze, plus goods from across the region.

tips.t: Besides metal, the wreck held Baltic amber, African blackwood, elephant and hippo ivory, ostrich eggshells and a gold scarab bearing Nefertiti's name: goods from nine or ten cultures.
A sponge diver found it in 1982, sketching 'metal biscuits with ears' (copper ingots). Excavating it 44–52 m down took eleven seasons and 22,413 dives.

steps.c: In 1274 BCE Ramesses II of Egypt and the Hittite king Muwatalli II fought at Kadesh on the Orontes, one of the largest chariot battles known. Both sides claimed victory; historians see a stalemate.

tips.t: Two nomads told Ramesses the Hittite army was far away near Aleppo. Captured spies then revealed it was hidden close by, and the Hittite chariots struck his marching army.
Sherden sea raiders, defeated by Ramesses II a few years earlier, fought for Egypt here; he took many into his personal guard.

steps.c: About 1259 BCE Ramesses II and Hattusili III agreed a treaty of peace and mutual help. It is the oldest known surviving peace treaty; a copy hangs at the United Nations.

tips.t: The Hittite copies, three clay tablets in Akkadian, were found in Hattusa's royal archive. The oath calls on a thousand gods; both sides promised to return each other's refugees.
In the 34th year of his reign Ramesses II married a Hittite princess. His delta capital Pi-Ramesses had stables with about 460 horse tether points.

steps.c: Tree rings from Anatolia point to a severe dry spell around 1198–1196 BCE. Drought, famine, earthquakes, raiders and fragile palace economies are all proposed causes; how much each mattered is debated.

tips.t: At the end of the second millennium BCE, the subsurface water level around the Dead Sea dropped by more than 50 metres, a sign of a drying climate.
At Kition on Cyprus the excavator found no evidence of violent destruction. One recent count argues 61% of claimed destructions around 1200 BCE are misdated or unproven (debated).

steps.c: The rich trading port of Ugarit in Syria was destroyed about 1190–1185 BCE and never rebuilt. Its scribes had used one of the earliest alphabets, written in cuneiform signs on clay.

tips.t: Ugarit's last king, Ammurapi, wrote to the king of Cyprus (Alashiya) that seven enemy ships had come and damaged his land. The city held about 7,000–8,000 people.
Ugarit was forgotten until a peasant ploughing a field in 1928 opened an old tomb. At its port, excavators found murex shells used to make purple dye.

steps.c: Hattusa, capital of the Hittite empire, was abandoned around 1180 BCE. Archaeologists think the court and elite left over decades; the fire found in the ruins probably came after.

tips.t: About 30,000 clay tablets from Hattusa form the main body of Hittite writing. The city covered 1.8 km² inside more than 6 km of walls.
Centuries earlier King Anitta left a curse on anyone who resettled the town: 'let the Stormgod of the Sky strike him!' The Hittites made it their capital anyway.

steps.c: Around 1180 BCE fire destroyed the palace at Pylos in Greece, as other Mycenaean palaces fell. The blaze baked its clay Linear B tablets, preserving the palace's records.

tips.t: The palace's wall paintings, long called frescoes, turned out to be egg tempera, among the oldest examples of this paint in the world.
In 2015 archaeologists found an untouched warrior's grave near the palace, an earlier Mycenaean burial with gold rings and bronze weapons.

steps.c: In his 8th year, about 1179–1175 BCE, Ramesses III fought invaders by land and sea near the Nile Delta. His temple at Medinet Habu shows the battle; who the 'Sea Peoples' were is still debated.

tips.t: Ramesses III's temple reliefs show the invaders with women and children in ox carts, suggesting migrants rather than just raiders. Its walls carry over 7,000 m² of reliefs.
Ramesses' inscription says no land could resist them, 'from Hatti, Kode, Carchemish, Arzawa, Alashiya'. Reliefs show enemy dead counted by piling up their severed hands.

steps.c: Greece entered a 'Dark Age' (about 1180–800 BCE) and lost writing. Phoenician cities such as Byblos thrived; by about 1000 BCE they used an alphabet that the Greeks later adapted, ancestor of Latin letters.

tips.t: Byblos traded so much Egyptian papyrus that the Greek word 'byblos' came to mean papyrus; English 'Bible' ultimately comes from the city's name.
The alphabet had 22 letters, all consonants, written right to left. Aleph meant 'ox' and bet 'house'; the Greeks later added vowels.

title: Rome: from village to empire and fall
blurb: From huts on the Palatine Hill to an empire around the Mediterranean, its long division, and the end of its eastern half in 1453.

steps.c: Legend says Romulus founded Rome in 753 BCE, a date fixed later by the scholar Varro. Archaeology shows hilltop villages with huts on the Palatine in the 9th–8th centuries BCE that slowly grew together.

tips.t: The valley below was marshy. The Cloaca Maxima drain, traditionally begun around 600 BCE, carried water to the Tiber, and part of it still drains central Rome today.
Emperors later built their homes on this hill, the Palatium, and its name gave English the word 'palace'.

steps.c: Tradition dates the overthrow of the last king and the start of the Republic to 509 BCE. Many historians think the real story was an aristocratic coup and the date is approximate.

tips.t: Livy says the Temple of Jupiter on the Capitol was dedicated on 13 September of the Republic's first year. Its terracotta statues were credited to Vulca, an Etruscan from Veii.
The king's powers passed to two consuls, elected for one year, each able to veto the other. A plebeian first became consul only in 366 BCE.

steps.c: By 264 BCE Rome dominated Italy south of the Po and began the Punic Wars with Carthage. In 216 BCE Hannibal destroyed a Roman army at Cannae, yet Rome fought on and won.

tips.t: Livy says Hannibal's brother Mago poured out a heap of gold rings in Carthage's senate, one for each Roman knight killed at Cannae.
Ancient counts of Roman dead range from 48,200 (Livy) to 70,000 (Polybius). The consul Varro reportedly escaped with about 70 horsemen.

steps.c: In spring 146 BCE, after a three-year siege, Roman troops destroyed Carthage and sold about 50,000 survivors into slavery. Its land became the province of Africa.

tips.t: Carthage's main land wall was 9 m wide and 15–20 m high, with barracks inside it for over 24,000 soldiers.
The famous story that Rome sowed Carthage's fields with salt is probably a 19th-century invention. Augustus later completed a new Roman city on the site.

steps.c: From 58 to 50 BCE Julius Caesar conquered Gaul, defeating Vercingetorix at Alesia in 52 BCE. Ancient figures of a million dead are seen as exaggerated, but the toll was huge.

tips.t: At Alesia Caesar built a 16 km ring of walls facing the town and a 21 km ring facing outward, with hidden pits and sharpened stakes in front.
The Gallic leader was held in Rome for five years, paraded in Caesar's triumph and then strangled in 46 BCE.

steps.c: In January 27 BCE the Senate gave Octavian the title Augustus. Rome kept the forms of the Republic but was ruled by one man, and a long era of relative peace, the Pax Romana, began.

tips.t: Augustus's ally Agrippa built the first Pantheon in 29–19 BCE. Hadrian rebuilt it later but kept Agrippa's name on the front, where it still stands.
Augustus was born Gaius Octavius on the Palatine Hill in 63 BCE. He ruled for about 41 years, and the month of August is named after him.

steps.c: Under Trajan (98–117 CE) the empire reached its greatest size, adding Dacia and, briefly, Armenia and Mesopotamia. His successor Hadrian soon gave up the eastern conquests.

tips.t: To invade Dacia, Trajan's architect Apollodorus built a 1,135 m bridge on 20 stone piers across the Danube in 103–105 CE. Two end pillars survive.
Trajan's Column in Rome tells the Dacian Wars in a 190 m spiral frieze with 2,662 figures; Trajan appears 58 times. His ashes were placed in its base.

steps.c: Between 235 and 284 CE dozens of emperors rose and fell amid civil wars, invasions, plague and a debased currency. The empire split into three parts until Aurelian reunited it by 274.

tips.t: After an invasion in 270, Aurelian walled Rome: 19 km long, with 383 towers by 500 CE. They defended the city until 1870.

steps.t: A new Rome in the East
steps.c: Diocletian (from 284) shared power among four rulers. Constantine reunited the empire and on 11 May 330 dedicated Constantinople, the rebuilt Byzantium, as its new capital.

tips.t: The Hippodrome, about 450 m long, held around 100,000 spectators. Constantine brought the bronze Serpent Column from Delphi to decorate it; its base still stands.
From 332 the new capital handed out free food like old Rome: about 80,000 rations a day from 117 distribution points.

steps.c: After Theodosius I died in 395 the empire was split between his sons, East and West. On 24 August 410 Alaric's Visigoths sacked Rome, the first foreign capture of the city in almost 800 years.

tips.t: To lift an earlier siege, Rome paid Alaric 5,000 pounds of gold, 30,000 of silver, 4,000 silk tunics, 3,000 scarlet hides and 3,000 pounds of pepper.
Alaric died of illness at Consentia (Cosenza) later in 410. Legend says slaves buried him with treasure in the bed of the Busento river, then were killed.

steps.c: In 476 Odoacer deposed the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus and sent the regalia to Constantinople. Historians debate whether this was a 'fall' or a gradual transformation into new kingdoms.
steps.w: Fall of the Western Roman Empire

tips.t: Odoacer spared the deposed emperor, gave him a pension of 6,000 solidi a year and sent him to Castellum Lucullanum near Naples, today's Castel dell'Ovo.
'Augustulus' was a mocking nickname for an emperor perhaps only ten years old. His father Orestes had once been secretary to Attila the Hun.

steps.c: The Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire lasted almost a thousand years more. On 29 May 1453 the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople, ending it.

tips.t: Orban's giant bombard was about 8.2 m long and hurled 270 kg stone balls over 1.6 km. Sixty oxen and 400 men dragged it; reloading took three hours.
A chain blocked the Golden Horn, so on 22 April Mehmed had his ships dragged on greased logs over the hill of Galata into the harbour.

title: The Mongol conquests
blurb: How the steppe tribes united under Genghis Khan built the largest contiguous land empire in history, from Korea to Hungary, and how it split into four khanates.

steps.c: After uniting the Mongol and Turkic tribes of the steppe, Temüjin was proclaimed Genghis Khan at a kurultai (great assembly) at the source of the Onon River in 1206. This is the usual founding date of the Mongol Empire.

tips.t: No one is sure what 'Genghis' meant: perhaps 'firm' or 'righteous', or from Turkic tängiz, 'ocean' – a ruler as wide as the world-encircling sea (debated).
He broke up the old tribes: every man aged 15 to 70 joined units of 10, 100 and 1,000. Commanders like Jelme and Subutai were blacksmiths' sons.

steps.c: The Mongols invaded Western Xia in 1209, which became a vassal in 1210, then turned on the Jin dynasty of northern China. The Jin capital Zhongdu, today's Beijing, surrendered on 31 May 1215.
steps.w: Mongol conquest of the Jin dynasty

tips.t: Besieging the Xia capital in 1209, the Mongols tried to flood it by diverting the Yellow River. Their dike broke and flooded their own camp instead.
Zhongdu's walls were almost 15 m thick at the base, with 13 gates and over 900 watchtowers. The Mongols could not storm them, so they starved the city out.

steps.c: After the Khwarazmian Empire executed his envoys, Genghis Khan invaded in 1219. Bukhara, Samarkand (March 1220) and Urgench fell, with huge massacres; medieval death tolls in the millions are considered exaggerated by modern historians, but the losses were enormous.
steps.w: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire

tips.t: Bukhara, mostly wooden, burned with its 45,000-book library. The Mongols razed the great mosque but left its Kalyan minaret, 45.6 m tall, built in 1127. It still stands.
Samarkand had eight iron gates and a garrison with 20 war elephants. To surprise Bukhara first, Genghis crossed the Kyzylkum Desert, thought impassable for an army.

steps.c: Two generals, Subutai and Jebe, led a long raid around the Caspian Sea and through the Caucasus. On 31 May 1223 they defeated an army of Rus' princes and Cumans at the Kalka River, in today's eastern Ukraine.

tips.t: Derbent, the 'gate' between the Caspian and the Caucasus, was spared for 10 guides. The mountain crossing still cost the Mongols their siege engines and hundreds of men to cold.
Jebe and Subutai rode about 8,900 km in three years. After the Kalka, Prince Mstislav of Kiev and his nobles were crushed beneath the victors' feasting platform.

steps.c: Genghis Khan died in August 1227 while campaigning against Western Xia; his burial place is unknown. His son Ögedei was elected Great Khan in 1229, conquered the Jin by 1234, and in 1235 walled Karakorum as the imperial capital.

tips.t: An enslaved Parisian goldsmith, Guillaume Bouchier, made a silver tree for the palace. When a mechanical angel blew its trumpet, serpents round the trunk gushed drinks.
Genghis Khan was buried on or near the sacred peak Burkhan Khaldun. The mountain was declared 'Great Taboo', closed to everyone except its guards.

steps.c: Batu and Subutai conquered the Rus' principalities, sacking Kyiv on 6 December 1240. In April 1241 they crushed a Polish army at Legnica and the Hungarians at Mohi, two days apart.

tips.t: In Kyiv, people crowded into the Church of the Tithes; its balcony collapsed under them. Of about 50,000 inhabitants, some 2,000 survived; six of forty major buildings stood.
At Legnica the Mongols reportedly cut an ear from each fallen enemy to count the dead, filling nine sacks – a figure as doubtful as European counts of Mongols.

steps.c: In 1242 the Mongols pulled back from Central Europe. The traditional reason is Ögedei's death in December 1241; historians debate this and also point to losses, strong stone castles, supply problems and wet, poor pasture.

tips.t: The Mongols looked set to stay: they named a governor (darughachi) for Hungary and minted coins in the Great Khan's name. Up to half of Hungary's people may have died.

tips.h: A princess born in a fortress
tips.t: Hunting King Béla IV, Mongol riders reached the Adriatic. His daughter Margaret, later a saint, was born in 1242 in Klis Fortress near Split.

steps.c: Hulagu, a grandson of Genghis Khan, besieged Baghdad, and the last Abbasid caliph surrendered on 10 February 1258. The city was sacked; estimates of the dead range from about 200,000 to over a million and are debated.

tips.t: Chroniclers said so many books from Baghdad's libraries, the House of Wisdom among them, were thrown into the Tigris that it ran black with ink. Historians suspect a literary trope.
Spilling royal blood was taboo to the Mongols, so the last caliph was reportedly rolled up in a carpet and trampled to death by horses.

steps.c: On 3 September 1260 the Mamluks of Egypt under Qutuz and Baybars defeated a Mongol army in the Jezreel Valley. It was the first major halt to the Mongol advance, and the Mongols withdrew from the Levant.

tips.t: Ain Jalut is a spring at the foot of Mount Gilboa, today Ma'ayan Harod. The Mongols camped there for water and pasture for their horses.
Most Mamluks were Kipchaks, Turkic slave soldiers from the steppe, many shipped from the Golden Horde's own lands via Black Sea ports. Steppe horsemen beat steppe horsemen.

steps.c: After Möngke died in 1259, a civil war between his brothers Kublai and Ariq Böke (1260–1264) broke the empire's unity. It split into the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate, the Ilkhanate in Iran and Kublai's realm in China.

tips.t: Russian princes, even the grand prince of Vladimir, had to travel to Sarai on the lower Volga to swear loyalty and receive the khan's patent (yarlyk) to rule.
Berke of the Golden Horde had become a Muslim and was horrified by his cousin Hulagu's sack of Baghdad. From 1262 to 1265 the two khans fought each other.

steps.c: Kublai proclaimed the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and took the Song capital Hangzhou in 1276. The last Song forces were destroyed in the naval Battle of Yamen on 19 March 1279, uniting China under Mongol rule.

tips.t: The Song chained about 1,000 ships together and coated them with fire-resistant mud against fire ships. Chained, they could neither help each other nor escape.
When all was lost, chancellor Lu Xiufu jumped into the sea with the boy emperor Zhao Bing. The child's body was reportedly found near today's Shekou in Shenzhen.

steps.c: Yuan fleets attacked Hakata Bay in Kyushu in 1274 and 1281. Japanese defences, including a stone wall, held, and in 1281 a typhoon wrecked the fleet: the 'kamikaze' or divine wind. Traditional army sizes are thought exaggerated.

tips.t: Divers found bomb shells in a Yuan shipwreck off Japan's coast. X-rays show gunpowder packed with scrap iron: the 'thunder crash bombs' fired by catapult.
The samurai Takezaki Suenaga had two illustrated scrolls made of his deeds in 1274 and 1281 – some of the earliest pictures of the invasions.

steps.c: Mongol rule made the Silk Road safer for trade, envoys and ideas. Marco Polo left Venice in 1271 and returned in 1295 after years at Kublai's court; how much of his book is first-hand is debated.

tips.t: Yam relay stations, about 32–64 km apart, kept fresh horses and food. Changing mounts, Mongol messengers covered 200–300 km a day.
Envoys carried a paiza, a tablet entitling them to horses and rations on the road. Not a Mongol invention: the Liao and Jin had used them before.

title: The Black Death
blurb: Follow the deadliest pandemic in recorded history from Central Asia across the Black Sea and the Mediterranean to every corner of Europe and the Middle East, 1338–1353.

steps.c: Ancient DNA from graves near Lake Issyk-Kul in Kyrgyzstan, where inscriptions record 'pestilence' deaths in 1338–1339, contains the plague bacterium Yersinia pestis. This strain is the direct ancestor of the Black Death strains (Spyrou et al. 2022).

tips.t: The victims lay in two Chüy Valley cemeteries of Nestorian Christians. Their Syriac tombstones give each name, the year of death and often the cause.
Plague lives on in the fleas of ground rodents; on the Central Asian steppes the main host is believed to be the marmot. Nearby Issyk-Kul is salty and rarely freezes.

steps.c: The Golden Horde besieged the Genoese port of Caffa in Crimea. One Italian writer, who was not there, reported that the Mongols catapulted plague corpses over the walls; historians debate this, and grain ships may have spread it instead.

tips.t: Italian merchants here shipped Turkic slaves to Egypt's Mamluk army. Angered, the khan Toqta besieged Caffa; in 1308 the Genoese burned it and left, returning later.
The war began with a brawl between Italians and Muslims in Tana, a Venetian post at the mouth of the Don. Jani Beg first besieged Caffa in 1343.

steps.c: Ships carried the disease across the Black Sea. It reached Constantinople in summer 1347 and Alexandria in Egypt that autumn, and spread along the trade routes of the eastern Mediterranean.

tips.t: In Constantinople the plague killed the 13-year-old son of Emperor John VI Kantakouzenos, who described it on the model of Thucydides' Plague of Athens.
Plague reached Alexandria in autumn 1347 by sea from Constantinople – on a single merchant ship carrying slaves.

steps.c: Twelve Genoese galleys brought plague to Messina in Sicily in October 1347. By early 1348 it was in Marseille, Pisa and Florence, and Venice by April. Boccaccio described the horror in Florence.

tips.t: In Boccaccio's Decameron, seven young women and three young men flee plague-struck Florence to a villa and tell 100 tales over ten days.
In Siena, the chronicler Agnolo di Tura saw bodies thrown into pits; no one cried, as all expected to die. The painters Ambrogio and Pietro Lorenzetti died too.

steps.c: Damascus, Aleppo and Mecca were struck. In Cairo, plague arrived in September 1348 and killed about a third of the people. Estimates for the Middle East are about one third overall.
steps.w: Black Death in the Middle East

tips.t: Cairo, with some 600,000 people the largest city of the Mediterranean, had a great hospital. Yet the boy sultan an-Nasir Hasan fled, and the Nile was choked with corpses.
In Gaza people fled to the countryside, the looters who plundered their homes died, and peasants reportedly fell dead in their fields while ploughing.

steps.c: The plague reached the Paris area in June 1348 and Melcombe (Weymouth) in England shortly before 24 June. London was hit that autumn. For England, 40–60% mortality is a widely accepted estimate.

tips.t: About half of Paris's 100,000 people are thought to have died. Florence shrank from some 110,000–120,000 people in 1338 to 50,000 in 1351.
At London's East Smithfield plague cemetery, 200 bodies a day were buried in mass graves, stacked five deep. DNA from these skeletons confirmed Yersinia pestis.

steps.c: Jews were falsely accused of poisoning wells. On 14 February 1349 much of Strasbourg's Jewish community, reportedly about 2,000 people, was burned; communities in Mainz, Cologne and hundreds of other towns were destroyed.

tips.t: Strasbourg's council had guarded the Jewish quarter; it was overthrown and replaced. Many who pushed the coup owed money to Jews and were rid of their debts.
King Casimir III of Poland gave Jews refuge and protection. Many fled east to Poland and Lithuania, where their communities remained for six centuries.

steps.c: Plague reached Oslo and, in late summer 1349, Bergen by ship from England, then spread north to Trondheim. Norway may have lost up to about 60% of its people and took centuries to recover.

tips.t: All of Norway's bishops except Oslo's died. By 1371, only 40 of the country's 300 priests were left.
With Norway's merchants weakened, German traders of the Hanseatic League took over Bergen's trade, and Germans replaced many dead Norwegian officials.

steps.c: Plague reached Pskov and Novgorod in 1352 and Moscow in 1353. Grand Prince Simeon the Proud, his sons and the Metropolitan of Moscow all died of it.

tips.t: Before he died, Simeon the Proud took monastic vows under the name Sozont. His brother Andrey outlived him by only six weeks.

steps.c: Estimates for Europe range from about 25% to 60% of the population, tens of millions of people. Labour became scarce and wages rose; England's Statute of Labourers (1351) tried to freeze them. Plague returned again and again until the 1600s–1700s.

tips.t: In 1377 Ragusa (Dubrovnik) made arrivals from plague areas wait 30 days, later 40. From Italian for 'forty' comes our word quarantine.
As early as 1351, agents of Pope Clement VI in Avignon counted 23,840,000 dead in Christian Europe – about 31% of some 75 million people.

title: The Reformation
blurb: How a dispute over indulgences split Western Christianity, redrew Europe's religious map and set off a century of reform, persecution and war.

steps.c: A century before Luther, the Prague preacher Jan Hus attacked the sale of indulgences and the wealth of the clergy, inspired by the English theologian John Wycliffe. He came to the Council of Constance under a promise of safe conduct, was arrested, and was burned as a heretic on 6 July 1415. Bohemia rose in the Hussite revolt, and in 1436 the Church accepted that Hussites could take communion in both bread and wine. Their church lasted until the Habsburgs suppressed it after 1620.

tips.t: The Council of Constance also condemned John Wycliffe, who had died in 1384. In 1428 his remains (or a neighbour's) were dug up at Lutterworth, burned and thrown into a river.
Radical Hussites founded their own town in 1420 and named it after the biblical Mount Tabor. In Czech, 'tábor' later came to mean 'camp'.

steps.img: Tour: A preacher burned at Constance

steps.t: Ninety-five theses and a printing press
steps.c: On 31 October 1517 Martin Luther, a monk and professor at the small university of Wittenberg, sent 95 theses against the sale of indulgences to the Archbishop of Mainz. Whether he also nailed them to a church door is debated. Printing made him famous: the movable-type press, introduced by Gutenberg in Mainz around 1450, had spread across Europe, and by 1520 Luther was Europe's most published author, with about 300,000 copies of his works in print.

tips.t: Gutenberg's first Bibles were finished in Mainz in 1454 or 1455. Of about 160 to 185 copies, 49 survive at least in large part.
The indulgences sold by the friar Johann Tetzel, which provoked Luther, partly paid for the new St Peter's Basilica in Rome.

steps.img: Tour: Ninety-five theses and a printing press

steps.c: In April 1521 Luther was summoned before the 21-year-old Emperor Charles V at the Diet of Worms and refused to recant his writings. The famous words 'Here I stand, I can do no other' may not be his: scholars consider the evidence for them unreliable. The Edict of Worms made him an outlaw, and his protector, Elector Frederick the Wise, had him secretly taken to the Wartburg castle for his safety.

tips.t: Hidden at the Wartburg as 'Junker Jörg' (Knight George), Luther translated the New Testament from Greek into German in about ten weeks; it was printed in September 1522.
While Luther was hidden, Andreas Karlstadt held the first Protestant communion in Wittenberg on Christmas Day 1521.

steps.img: Tour: Here I stand

steps.c: In Zürich the priest Huldrych Zwingli, working independently of Luther, won over the city council at a public disputation on 29 January 1523. Images were removed and the Mass abolished; the break had begun in 1522 when Zwingli defended friends who ate sausages during Lent. Some of his students wanted more: in January 1525 they baptised each other as adults, starting the Anabaptist movement. Catholic and Protestant rulers alike persecuted Anabaptists; in 1527 Zürich drowned Felix Manz, the first Swiss Anabaptist martyr.

tips.t: Zwingli went to war with the Catholic cantons and was killed at the Battle of Kappel in 1531; Switzerland stayed divided between Reformed and Catholic cantons.
At the Marburg Colloquy of 1529 Luther and Zwingli agreed on 14 of 15 articles but not on the Lord's Supper, and the Protestant camp stayed split.

steps.img: Tour: Zürich goes further

steps.c: Many peasants heard the new preaching as a call for justice. In March 1525 their Twelve Articles, drafted in Memmingen, demanded the right to choose their own pastors and an end to serfdom. About 300,000 poorly armed peasants rose across southern and central Germany; the princes' armies crushed them and killed up to 100,000. Luther condemned the revolt and urged the princes to strike the rebels down. The radical preacher Thomas Müntzer was captured at Frankenhausen and executed.

tips.t: The Twelve Articles were printed more than 25,000 times within two months, and they are often called the first draft of human rights in continental Europe.
Thomas Müntzer organised an armed militia in the imperial city of Mühlhausen; after the defeat at Frankenhausen he was executed outside its walls on 27 May 1525.

steps.img: Tour: The Peasants' War

steps.c: German princes and city councils now introduced the Reformation themselves, issuing church orders and closing monasteries. When the Diet of Speyer tried to stop them in 1529, six princes and 14 imperial cities protested, which gave us the word 'Protestant'. At Augsburg on 25 June 1530 they presented the Augsburg Confession to Charles V. Drafted mainly by Philip Melanchthon, it is still the basic statement of Lutheran faith.

tips.t: In 1525 Albert, Grand Master of the Teutonic Knights, turned the order's lands into the Duchy of Prussia, the first state to adopt Lutheranism officially.
Nuremberg accepted the Reformation in 1525. In 1532 the Nuremberg Religious Peace, signed there, kept Lutherans and Catholics from war for 15 years.

steps.img: Tour: Princes and cities protest

steps.c: Henry VIII wanted his marriage to Catherine of Aragon annulled, and the Pope refused. On 3 November 1534 Parliament's Act of Supremacy made the King head of the Church of England, and between 1536 and 1541 every monastery in England and Wales was dissolved. The country then swung back and forth: Edward VI pushed Protestantism further, Mary I restored Catholicism and burned at least 280 Protestants, and Elizabeth I settled a Protestant Church of England from 1559.

tips.t: William Tyndale's English New Testament had to be printed abroad. He was strangled and burned at Vilvoorde near Brussels in 1536, yet much of the King James Bible's New Testament (estimates 55–83%) keeps his words.
Scotland took a different path: in 1560 its Parliament broke with Rome, and John Knox shaped a Presbyterian, largely Calvinist Church of Scotland.

steps.img: Tour: England breaks with Rome

steps.t: Kings take over the Nordic churches
steps.c: In Scandinavia kings led the Reformation and took over the Church's lands. Gustav Vasa of Sweden broke the bishops' power at the 'Reformation Riksdag' of Västerås in 1527, though Sweden only fixed its Lutheran creed in 1593. Christian III of Denmark arrested his bishops in 1536 after a civil war, the Count's Feud, and made Lutheranism official across Denmark–Norway. These state churches lasted into modern times: Sweden separated church and state only in 2000.

tips.t: Jón Arason, the last Catholic bishop in Iceland, fought the Danish Reformation with his sons. He and two of them were captured and beheaded at Skálholt on 7 November 1550.
Mikael Agricola, later bishop of Turku, printed the first Finnish book, an ABC primer, in 1543, and the Finnish New Testament in 1548. He is called the father of literary Finnish.

steps.img: Tour: Kings take over the Nordic churches

steps.c: Geneva voted for the Reformation in 1536, the year the young French exile John Calvin published his Institutes and arrived in the city. Expelled in 1538, he returned on 13 September 1541 and built a disciplined church, with a Consistory of ministers and elders that judged church matters. Geneva also burned the anti-Trinitarian Michael Servetus in 1553. Its Academy (1559) trained pastors for France, the Netherlands, Scotland and beyond, and Calvinism became an international movement.

tips.t: English Protestant exiles in Geneva produced the Geneva Bible (1560), the main Bible of Elizabethan England; Shakespeare, Knox and Cromwell used it, and it sailed on the Mayflower.
Debrecen in eastern Hungary turned Reformed so early and so firmly that it was nicknamed the 'Calvinist Rome'.

steps.img: Tour: Calvin's Geneva

steps.c: The Catholic Church reformed itself too, building on renewal movements older than Luther. The Council of Trent met in 25 sessions between 13 December 1545 and 1563. It restated Catholic doctrine against the Protestants, and it reformed the training of priests and required bishops to live in their dioceses. New orders carried the renewal, above all the Jesuits, approved in 1540, who founded schools throughout Europe and sent missionaries worldwide. Rome also set up the Roman Inquisition in 1542.

tips.t: Ignatius of Loyola was a Basque soldier whose leg was shattered by a cannonball at Pamplona on 20 May 1521. Reading the lives of saints while he recovered changed his life.
In 1562 Teresa of Ávila founded the first of her reformed Carmelite convents. In 1970 she was the first woman named a Doctor of the Church.

steps.img: Tour: The Catholic Reformation

steps.c: Charles V finally went to war against the Protestant Schmalkaldic League and won at Mühlberg on 24 April 1547, but he could not undo the Reformation. The Peace of Augsburg, signed on 25 September 1555, let each prince choose Lutheranism or Catholicism for his land, later summed up as 'cuius regio, eius religio' (whose realm, his religion).
