tips.t: Byron wrote his poem "Darkness" after a day when "the fowls all went to roost at noon" and candles were lit as at midnight. Mary Shelley was just 18.
The cold let an ice dam form below the Giétro Glacier in the Val de Bagnes. Despite drainage work it burst in June 1818, killing forty people.

steps.c: Famine struck eastern Switzerland in 1816–17. In south-western Germany more people left than died: many emigrated to America, and Swabian groups trekked to the Russian Caucasus (1817–19), though religion also drove them.

tips.t: Justus von Liebig lived through the famine as a child in Darmstadt. He later studied plant nutrition and introduced mineral fertilizers.
Floods made major rivers like the Rhine hard to navigate, slowing grain shipments; prices rose most in inland German lands.

steps.c: Hunger weakened people and a typhus epidemic swept Ireland from 1816 to 1819, spreading on to Britain and the continent. Estimates put the deaths at about 65,000.

tips.t: Cold and heavy rain ruined British harvests. Families in Wales walked long distances as refugees, begging for food.
The Central England temperature record, kept since 1659, logged 1816 as its coldest July and third coldest summer.

steps.c: The Indian monsoon came late, then brought torrential rain. In 1817 cholera broke out near Jessore in Bengal and became the first cholera pandemic, reaching Southeast Asia, China and Arabia. Whether Tambora helped trigger it is debated.

tips.t: The disturbed seasons even brought abnormal cold and snow to Bengal during the winter monsoon.
Cholera reached Calcutta by September 1817. About 10,000 troops in British service died in the pandemic, which drew Europe's attention.

steps.c: On 12 June 1817 Karl Drais rode his wooden running machine from Mannheim, an ancestor of the bicycle. Oats were scarce and many horses died after 1816; that this inspired Drais is a popular idea but debated.

tips.t: The rider pushed off the ground with his feet, with no pedals. On level ground the machine reached about 16 km/h, more than double walking pace.
Drais patented it in France in February 1818 as the vélocipède. In the 1860s French makers added cranks and pedals to the front wheel.

steps.c: Volcanic haze makes sunsets glow red and yellow. J. M. W. Turner's golden skies, such as Chichester Canal (1828), may reflect such sunsets; a 2007 study found redder skies in paintings after big eruptions. The link is plausible, not proven.

tips.t: Already in 1815 Londoners saw long, brilliant sunsets, orange or red near the horizon and purple above, from 28 June to 2 July and again in autumn.
The 3rd Earl of Egremont commissioned Chichester Canal. The ship is probably a collier brig; the final version of the scene hangs at Petworth House.

title: Volcanoes that changed the climate
blurb: Seven eruptions, from the dark sun of 536 to Pinatubo in 1991, that cooled the planet and shook harvests and societies.

steps.c: In 536 the historian Procopius wrote that the sun shone without brightness for a year. European summers were up to about 2.5 °C colder. Ice cores point to eruptions in North America, but the exact volcanoes are debated.

tips.t: Tree rings from Irish oaks, studied by Mike Baillie in Belfast, show abnormally little growth in 536 and another sharp drop in 542.
Glass shards in ice cores dated to 536 point to three North American eruptions; one matches tephra from the Mono Craters in California.

steps.t: A Late Antique Little Ice Age
steps.c: A second eruption around 539–540 cooled summers again, and the cold lasted until about 660. Famine and the Plague of Justinian, first seen in Egypt in 541, followed; how far the climate helped the plague is debated.

tips.t: From about 540 the people of Elusa, a Negev city of tens of thousands, made less and less rubbish: a sign the city was shrinking.
Archaeologists think Scandinavia may have lost up to half its people after the eruptions of 536–547. The disaster may be the origin of the Norse "Fimbulwinter".

steps.c: Ice cores showed a huge sulfur spike around 1257, but no known volcano matched. In 2013 scientists traced it to Samalas on Lombok, whose eruption (VEI 7) buried the town of Pamatan. Its climate effects were milder than models suggest.

tips.t: The Babad Lombok, written on palm leaves in Old Javanese, says Pamatan had about 10,000 people and walls. Its king escaped, but the city's site is still lost.
Samalas may once have stood about 4,200 m high. Today its place is a 6–7 km wide caldera holding Lake Segara Anak, 200 m deep.

steps.c: On 19 February 1600 Huaynaputina in southern Peru erupted (VEI 6), the largest recorded eruption in South America. Ash collapsed roofs in Arequipa, wiped out local vineyards and killed about 1,000–1,500 people.

tips.t: In Lima and Arica people took the blasts for a naval fight with English corsairs, and the viceroy sent troops to Callao.
Between 11 and 17 villages within 20 km were buried. Estagagache is called the "Pompeii of Peru"; a project begun in 2015 is searching for the lost towns.

steps.c: The summer of 1601 was among the coldest in six centuries. Frosts ruined Russian harvests, and the famine of 1601–03 killed perhaps two million people, deepening the Time of Troubles. The eruption is a likely, not certain, cause.

tips.t: Tsar Boris Godunov sold state grain at half price, then gave grain and money away until the treasury ran dry. Still, 127,000 bodies went into Moscow's mass graves.
Deaths and failed crops in 1601–1603 led Estonians to abandon three quarters of all farms, at least for a time.

steps.c: From June 1783 the Laki fissure in Iceland poured out lava and gas for eight months. Fluorine poisoned the grass, most sheep died and the famine killed about a fifth of Icelanders. Sulfurous haze drifted over Europe, linked to about 23,000 deaths in Britain (estimate).

tips.t: On 20 July 1783 pastor Jón Steingrímsson preached his "fire mass" at Kirkjubæjarklaustur. The lava stopped short of the church, at a spot since called Fire Mass Point.
The cloud reached Prague by 17 June, Berlin by 18 June and Paris by 20 June. Ships stayed in port and the sun looked "blood coloured".

steps.c: The largest eruption in recorded history (VEI 7) made 1816 the "Year Without a Summer" around the Northern Hemisphere. Its full story has its own tour: Tambora and the Year Without a Summer.

tips.t: On 10 April 1815 people in Trumon, Sumatra, more than 2,600 km away, thought the explosions were the sound of firing guns.
Tambora stood about 4,300 m high, one of the tallest peaks in the archipelago. The eruption cut it to 2,851 m.

steps.c: On 27 August 1883 Krakatoa exploded in the Sunda Strait, heard 4,800 km away. Tsunamis killed most of at least 36,000 victims. Red sunsets circled the globe; cooling estimates range from about 0.4 to 1.2 °C.

tips.t: The loudest sound ever measured burst the eardrums of sailors on the ship Norham Castle, about 64 km away off Sumatra.
Pumice from the eruption floated across the Indian Ocean for almost a year before washing ashore at Takwa Beach in Kenya.

steps.c: On 15 June 1991 Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines erupted (VEI 6); evacuations saved many, but 847 died. Satellites tracked its sulfur haze, and the world cooled by about 0.4–0.5 °C for two years, as predicted.

tips.t: Typhoon Yunya struck on the same day, passing about 75 km north. Its rain soaked the falling ash, so roofs collapsed and mudflows poured down.
The Aeta living on the volcano's slopes left their villages when the first blasts began in April; some moved up to nine times in two months.

title: The 4.2-kiloyear drought
blurb: Around 2200 BCE a dry, cool spell hit many regions, and several early states and cities declined at about the same time, though how much the climate caused is debated.

steps.c: Liangzhu, a walled city with large dams near Hangzhou, was abandoned around 2300 BCE. Flood layers point to a very wet spell, not drought; whether this belongs to the 4.2 ka event is debated.

tips.t: Only one road crossed the walls. People travelled by boat on 30 km of moats and canals controlled by eight water gates.
The Fanshan and Jiangjiashan cemeteries held 4,229 jade objects. The largest jade cong (ritual tube) of the culture weighs 3.5 kg.

steps.t: A climate shift named in stone
steps.c: Since 2018 geologists start the Meghalayan stage, our current one, about 4,200 years ago. Its marker is a stalagmite in Mawmluh Cave, India, recording a drier monsoon. Whether the drought was truly global is debated.

tips.t: Mawmluh Cave in Meghalaya is a 7.2 km maze cave, the fourth longest on the subcontinent. In 2022 it joined the IUGS list of 100 geological heritage sites.
Around the Persian Gulf the 22nd-century BCE drought marks the end of the Umm Al Nar culture and the start of the Wadi Suq culture.

steps.c: Around 2200 BCE the Early Helladic II culture of mainland Greece ended; at Lerna the 'House of the Tiles' burned. Climate change may have contributed, but destructions were uneven and the link is uncertain.

tips.t: Lerna once lay beside a freshwater lagoon about 4.7 km across, where myth placed the many-headed Hydra. Silt turned it into marsh, drained in the 1800s.
Lerna's toolmakers worked obsidian shipped from Melos. Less of it arrived by the end of Early Helladic III, a sign of shrinking long-distance trade.

steps.c: Harvey Weiss found Tell Leilan in Syria abandoned during a long dry spell around 2200 BCE and linked it to the Akkadian Empire's fall (c. 2154 BCE). Many historians see the collapse as multi-causal; debated.

tips.t: Excavators found a layer of sediment about a metre (3 ft) thick at Tell Leilan with no trace of people living there.
Around 1800 BCE King Shamshi-Adad I revived the site as his capital Shubat-Enlil: 90 hectares, perhaps 20,000 people, and an archive of 1,100 tablets.

steps.c: After about 2181 BCE Egypt split into rival centres at Herakleopolis and Thebes: the First Intermediate Period. Very low Nile floods may have caused famine, but scholars have no consensus on that link.

tips.t: Warlord Ankhtifi's tomb at Mo'alla boasts that he gave bread to the hungry and let no one die. Many rulers made such claims; how bad the famine was is debated.
Pepi II, buried at Saqqara, ruled from childhood perhaps into his 90s (uncertain) and outlived many heirs, one reason given for the troubled succession.

steps.c: Mesopotamian tradition blamed the Gutians for ending Akkad. Utu-hengal of Uruk drove them out around 2119 BCE, and Ur-Nammu founded the Third Dynasty of Ur about 2112 BCE (middle chronology).

tips.t: Ur-Nammu built the ziggurat of the moon god Nanna: 64 by 45 m at the base, of mud brick faced with fired bricks set in bitumen.
About 120,000 clay tablets survive from Ur III, mostly receipts and accounts. The first big batch was dug up in 1894 at Girsu (Tello).

steps.c: Around 2000 BCE population fell and big Longshan centres were abandoned in most areas, possibly through environmental change; Taosi was deserted by about 1900 BCE. The central area led on to Erlitou. Causes are debated.

tips.t: At Taosi a semicircular rammed-earth platform has slots facing points on Chongfen Mountain where the sun rises; it was probably used to follow the solar calendar.
Longshan potters used the wheel to make thin-walled, polished black pottery; the "eggshell" cups of Shandong are the finest.

steps.c: From about 1900 BCE big Indus cities such as Mohenjo-daro emptied and people moved east into villages. A weaker monsoon and a shrinking Ghaggar-Hakra river are leading explanations, but their role is debated.

tips.t: Mohenjo-daro had over 700 wells, about one for every three houses, plus drains and bathing places: unheard of in Egypt or Mesopotamia then.
Steps lead down into a brick pool 12 m long, 7 m wide and 2.4 m deep, sealed with bitumen; it may have served for religious purification.

title: The Little Ice Age
blurb: From roughly 1300 to 1850 the Northern Hemisphere was often colder than before or since, with frozen rivers, advancing glaciers and famines; its dates and causes are still argued over.

steps.t: A cold age with fuzzy edges
steps.c: There is no agreed start or end: many use about 1300–1850, others the 16th–19th centuries. The huge 1257 Samalas eruption in Indonesia may have helped trigger it, though that is debated.

tips.t: Witnesses reported 15,000–20,000 deaths in London during the cold, wet 1258. A mass grave of famine victims was found in the city in the 1990s.
Tree rings record the chill: slower growth in Mongolia in 1258–1262, frost-damaged rings in Canada, and a decade of thin rings in Norway and Sweden.

steps.c: From 1315 to 1317 endless rain and cold ruined harvests across northern Europe; perhaps 10–25% of many towns' people died. It is often linked to the start of the Little Ice Age.

tips.t: On 10 August 1315 King Edward II stopped at St Albans and could hardly find bread for himself and his court.
Brine would not evaporate in the wet, so salt for curing meat grew scarce and dear. In Lorraine wheat prices rose by 320%.

steps.c: A wedding at Hvalsey Church in 1408 is the last written record of the Greenland Norse; the settlements faded during the 1400s. Colder, stormier seas, a falling ivory trade and rising sea level are all proposed; debated.

tips.t: Bones show the first settlers ate about 80% farm food. By the 1300s, 50–80% of the Greenlanders' diet came from the sea.
Hvalsey church was built of granite blocks, some of 4–5 tonnes, plastered with crushed-shell mortar that made it white. The 1408 couple later settled in Iceland.

steps.c: In the 'Grindelwald Fluctuation' (about 1560–1630) Alpine glaciers grew sharply and threatened farms. Volcanic eruptions such as Huaynaputina (1600) are one suspected cause.

tips.t: Temperatures were 1–2 °C below 20th-century averages. The glacier advance began about 15 years before the first big eruption (Colima, 1585).
In 2008 the Upper Grindelwald Glacier's tongue still reached down to about 1,400 m, one of the lowest glaciers in the Alps.

steps.t: Drought and the fall of Ming
steps.c: Severe drought hit north China in the 1630s amid famine and revolts. Li Zicheng's rebels took Beijing in April 1644 and the Qing soon followed. Climate was one factor among many; its weight is debated.

tips.t: As the rebels took Beijing, the Chongzhen Emperor hanged himself from a tree in the imperial garden outside the Forbidden City.
General Wu Sangui held Shanhai Pass, the Great Wall's eastern end. He joined the Manchus, whose cavalry routed Li Zicheng's army there on 27 May 1644.

steps.c: Wars, revolts and famines peaked across Eurasia in the mid-1600s, including the Thirty Years' War, ended in 1648. Geoffrey Parker links this to Little Ice Age cooling; whether there was one general crisis is debated.

tips.t: War was the norm in the 1600s: in the century Poland saw only 27 years of peace, the Dutch Republic 14, France 11 and Spain just 3.
Germany's population fell by about 15–30% during the Thirty Years' War.

steps.t: An army marches over the sea
steps.c: In February 1658 the winter was so hard that Charles X Gustav's Swedish army crossed the frozen Little and Great Belts to threaten Copenhagen. Denmark gave up Scania and other lands at Roskilde.

tips.t: Off Funen the ice broke behind the Swedes: two cavalry squadrons vanished, and the king's sled sank with its crew and horses. He had already mounted a horse.
At Nyborg four Danish ships under Vice Admiral Peter Bredal were frozen in. Asked to surrender, Bredal chose to fight.

steps.c: London held fairs on the frozen Thames from 1608 to 1814; the most famous was the Great Frost of 1683–84. It fell in the Maunder Minimum (1645–1715), when sunspots almost vanished; its role in the cooling is debated.

tips.t: For sixpence a printer named Croom sold cards with your name, the date and proof they were printed on the Thames. Charles II bought one.
Old London Bridge's 19 piers slowed the wide river so ice jammed. After it was replaced in 1831 and the banks built up, frost fairs ended.

steps.c: Cold summers and early frosts in 1695–97 brought the Great Famine: about a third of Finland's people and a fifth of Estonia's died. Sweden and Norway suffered too.

tips.t: About 150,000 of Finland's 500,000 people died in two years. Many relied on bread made with bark; some historians call them "the years of many deaths".
In 1695 Israel Kolmodin wrote the Swedish hymn "Den blomstertid nu kommer" as a prayer that the next summer would bring food.

steps.c: In the 1690s, Scotland's coldest decade in 750 years, harvests failed again and again; perhaps 5–15% of Scots starved. The crisis helped push Scotland towards union with England in 1707.

tips.t: So many starving beggars reached Edinburgh in December 1696 that the town council set up a "refugee camp" in Greyfriars kirkyard.
In 1698 oatmeal in Aberdeen cost two-thirds more than usual. People ate grass and nettles, and deaths in Aberdeenshire may have reached 25%.

steps.c: The 1815 eruption of Tambora cooled the globe for a year: June snow in New England and crop failures in Europe and China. See the Tambora tour for the full story.

tips.t: On 29–30 July 1816 a violent storm with hail and strong northerly winds struck near Cape Town, badly damaging shipping.
News from Pernambuco in February 1817 told of an uncommon drought in north-eastern Brazil: streams dry, cattle dying, people moving to the big rivers.

steps.c: After about 1850 glaciers worldwide began to shrink as the climate warmed; industrial soot may have sped up early Alpine retreat. Since the late 20th century, human greenhouse gases are the main driver.

tips.t: Tourists have walked through an ice grotto in the Rhône Glacier since 1870. Since 1850 it has lost about 60% of its volume; white blankets now slow the melt.
The Great Aletsch, the Alps' largest glacier, has retreated more than 4 km: its 19th-century snout lay where the Gibidum reservoir is now.
